* The 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans
Dariush Mozaffarian, MD, DrPH
On January 7, 2026,the US Department of Health and Human Ser￾vices and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) released the
2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGAs),1
which by law
are revised every 5 years. Interest in this update has been height￾ened by the Trump administration’s focus on food and health, prior
provocative statements on nutrition, departures from usual admin￾istrative and scientific processes in other areas (eg, vaccines), and
the Make America Healthy Again movement.
TheDGAs serve as the nation’s nutritional recommendations for
the general population and directly inform procurement standards
in schools and day-care facilities, other federal nutrition programs,
military nutrition, and federal cafeterias. The DGAs also influence in￾dustry formulationsandmarketing.A clear understanding of the con￾tents of the DGAs, their implications, and unanswered questions is
critical for those interested in patient care, public health, scientific
research, and policy.
First-Ever Limits on Processed Foods
Several updates to the DGAs1
are salient (Table). The most notable is
a major emphasis on limiting or avoiding foods that are highly pro￾cessed, packaged, or ready toeat; sugar-sweetened beverages; other
foods high in added sugars or sodium; and refined, highly processed
carbohydrates. These foods are consistently associated with ad￾verse health outcomes and arewidely overconsumed; refined grains,
for example, are themost problematic of this group and are overcon￾sumed by more than 95% of individuals in the US.2Yet, even though
groups such as the American Heart Association and prior indepen￾dent Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committees have advised against
such foods, no prior DGAs carried forward such recommendations.
Previously, the government appeared unwilling or unable to make
statements that might threaten sales of any particular food sector.
Instead, prior DGAs generally presented all food choices as ac￾ceptablewithin certain daily nutrient targets, such as for salt or sugar.
This implicitly permitted foods like soda and processedmeats within
a healthful pattern, provided that overall nutrient targets were
met—an approach inconsistent with evidence for harms of certain
products. In schoolmeals, for example, highly processed items such
as flavoredmilks, refined-grain entrées, processedmeats, and pack￾aged snack foods are permitted even though these do not pro￾mote optimal health.With this approach, there are no “bad foods”—a
strategy for nourishment of “everything in moderation” that defers
to industry interests.
Given this history, the wide range of foods to be avoided or lim￾ited in the newDGAs is remarkable.It includes not only sugary drinks,
but also chips, cookies, candy, white bread, packaged breakfast ce￾reals, crackers,meatswith chemicaladditives (like nitrites),andmore.
The update further advises, for the first time, limiting products with
artificial flavors, petroleum-based dyes, artificial preservatives, or
nonnutritive sweeteners. Limits on added sugar are also strength￾ened per product, per meal, and by age group, including new guid￾ance for zero intake of added sugar from birth through 10 years of
age.In sum, theDGAs advise against60% to70% of the current food
supply,3 a landmark change from prior iterations and an unmistak￾able signal to the food industry.
Encouraging More Whole Foods
A second positive update is the major focus on whole or minimally
processed foods, fiber-richwhole grains, and healthy fats. PriorDGAs
have included similar points, but not with the same emphasis. De￾ficiencies in these foods contribute to much of the chronic disease
burden in theUS.A relatedmajor change is thatwhole-fat dairy foods
with no added sugars can be included, which is consistent with the
accumulated evidence of no meaningful benefit in choosing low￾fat dairy over whole-fat dairy.2,4 When combined with new guid￾ance on highly processed foods, added sugars, artificial sweeten￾ers, and other additives—encapsulated in a new tagline, “eat real
food”—these changes could transform meals and snacks for chil￾dren (eg, away from flavored, low-fat milks or yogurts toward plain
whole-fat options and away from sweetened refined grain snacks
toward healthy oils and whole grains).
A shortcoming is insufficient nuance on the hierarchy of fat
sources. Plant, dairy, and animal sources are grouped together,
belying the evidence that plant and seafood sources provide the
greatest benefits, followed by dairy (especially fermented options
like yogurt or cheese), and that red and processed meats are less
salubrious, less due to their fat than other carcinogenic and pro￾inflammatory compounds.5 The DGAs mention butter and beef
tallow as options, but on a positive note recommend prioritizing
“oils with essential fatty acids, such as olive oil”1
and do not advise

* The 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans
Dariush Mozaffarian, MD, DrPH
On January 7, 2026,the US Department of Health and Human Ser￾vices and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) released the
2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGAs),1
which by law
are revised every 5 years. Interest in this update has been height￾ened by the Trump administration’s focus on food and health, prior
provocative statements on nutrition, departures from usual admin￾istrative and scientific processes in other areas (eg, vaccines), and
the Make America Healthy Again movement.
TheDGAs serve as the nation’s nutritional recommendations for
the general population and directly inform procurement standards
in schools and day-care facilities, other federal nutrition programs,
military nutrition, and federal cafeterias. The DGAs also influence in￾dustry formulationsandmarketing.A clear understanding of the con￾tents of the DGAs, their implications, and unanswered questions is
critical for those interested in patient care, public health, scientific
research, and policy.
First-Ever Limits on Processed Foods
Several updates to the DGAs1
are salient (Table). The most notable is
a major emphasis on limiting or avoiding foods that are highly pro￾cessed, packaged, or ready toeat; sugar-sweetened beverages; other
foods high in added sugars or sodium; and refined, highly processed
carbohydrates. These foods are consistently associated with ad￾verse health outcomes and arewidely overconsumed; refined grains,
for example, are themost problematic of this group and are overcon￾sumed by more than 95% of individuals in the US.2Yet, even though
groups such as the American Heart Association and prior indepen￾dent Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committees have advised against
such foods, no prior DGAs carried forward such recommendations.
Previously, the government appeared unwilling or unable to make
statements that might threaten sales of any particular food sector.
Instead, prior DGAs generally presented all food choices as ac￾ceptablewithin certain daily nutrient targets, such as for salt or sugar.
This implicitly permitted foods like soda and processedmeats within
a healthful pattern, provided that overall nutrient targets were
met—an approach inconsistent with evidence for harms of certain
products. In schoolmeals, for example, highly processed items such
as flavoredmilks, refined-grain entrées, processedmeats, and pack￾aged snack foods are permitted even though these do not pro￾mote optimal health.With this approach, there are no “bad foods”—a
strategy for nourishment of “everything in moderation” that defers
to industry interests.
Given this history, the wide range of foods to be avoided or lim￾ited in the newDGAs is remarkable.It includes not only sugary drinks,
but also chips, cookies, candy, white bread, packaged breakfast ce￾reals, crackers,meatswith chemicaladditives (like nitrites),andmore.
The update further advises, for the first time, limiting products with
artificial flavors, petroleum-based dyes, artificial preservatives, or
nonnutritive sweeteners. Limits on added sugar are also strength￾ened per product, per meal, and by age group, including new guid￾ance for zero intake of added sugar from birth through 10 years of
age.In sum, theDGAs advise against60% to70% of the current food
supply,3 a landmark change from prior iterations and an unmistak￾able signal to the food industry.
Encouraging More Whole Foods
A second positive update is the major focus on whole or minimally
processed foods, fiber-richwhole grains, and healthy fats. PriorDGAs
have included similar points, but not with the same emphasis. De￾ficiencies in these foods contribute to much of the chronic disease
burden in theUS.A relatedmajor change is thatwhole-fat dairy foods
with no added sugars can be included, which is consistent with the
accumulated evidence of no meaningful benefit in choosing low￾fat dairy over whole-fat dairy.2,4 When combined with new guid￾ance on highly processed foods, added sugars, artificial sweeten￾ers, and other additives—encapsulated in a new tagline, “eat real
food”—these changes could transform meals and snacks for chil￾dren (eg, away from flavored, low-fat milks or yogurts toward plain
whole-fat options and away from sweetened refined grain snacks
toward healthy oils and whole grains).
A shortcoming is insufficient nuance on the hierarchy of fat
sources. Plant, dairy, and animal sources are grouped together,
belying the evidence that plant and seafood sources provide the
greatest benefits, followed by dairy (especially fermented options
like yogurt or cheese), and that red and processed meats are less
salubrious, less due to their fat than other carcinogenic and pro￾inflammatory compounds.5 The DGAs mention butter and beef
tallow as options, but on a positive note recommend prioritizing
“oils with essential fatty acids, such as olive oil”1
and do not advise
against omega-6 fats or seed oils, which are oils that have been dis￾paraged in social media campaigns despite their well-established
health benefits.5
A Boost to Protein
A third major change is that the DGAs recommended higher di￾etary protein from the existing Dietary Reference Intake of 0.8 g/kg
of body weight per day to a target of 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg of body weight
per day. For an average adult, this change translates to approxi￾mately 16% to 21% of calories from protein, which is higher than
the current national average intake of 16%.6 Although dietary pro￾tein can increase muscle mass and strength when combined with
regular strength or resistance training, there is little evidence
that, absent sustained training, higher protein builds muscle or pro￾vides other health benefits.7,8 In fact, excess dietary protein can be
converted to fat by the liver, increasing visceral adiposity and dia￾betes risk.8,9

* The 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans
Dariush Mozaffarian, MD, DrPH
On January 7, 2026,the US Department of Health and Human Ser￾vices and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) released the
2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGAs),1
which by law
are revised every 5 years. Interest in this update has been height￾ened by the Trump administration’s focus on food and health, prior
provocative statements on nutrition, departures from usual admin￾istrative and scientific processes in other areas (eg, vaccines), and
the Make America Healthy Again movement.
TheDGAs serve as the nation’s nutritional recommendations for
the general population and directly inform procurement standards
in schools and day-care facilities, other federal nutrition programs,
military nutrition, and federal cafeterias. The DGAs also influence in￾dustry formulationsandmarketing.A clear understanding of the con￾tents of the DGAs, their implications, and unanswered questions is
critical for those interested in patient care, public health, scientific
research, and policy.
First-Ever Limits on Processed Foods
Several updates to the DGAs1
are salient (Table). The most notable is
a major emphasis on limiting or avoiding foods that are highly pro￾cessed, packaged, or ready toeat; sugar-sweetened beverages; other
foods high in added sugars or sodium; and refined, highly processed
carbohydrates. These foods are consistently associated with ad￾verse health outcomes and arewidely overconsumed; refined grains,
for example, are themost problematic of this group and are overcon￾sumed by more than 95% of individuals in the US.2Yet, even though
groups such as the American Heart Association and prior indepen￾dent Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committees have advised against
such foods, no prior DGAs carried forward such recommendations.
Previously, the government appeared unwilling or unable to make
statements that might threaten sales of any particular food sector.
Instead, prior DGAs generally presented all food choices as ac￾ceptablewithin certain daily nutrient targets, such as for salt or sugar.
This implicitly permitted foods like soda and processedmeats within
a healthful pattern, provided that overall nutrient targets were
met—an approach inconsistent with evidence for harms of certain
products. In schoolmeals, for example, highly processed items such
as flavoredmilks, refined-grain entrées, processedmeats, and pack￾aged snack foods are permitted even though these do not pro￾mote optimal health.With this approach, there are no “bad foods”—a
strategy for nourishment of “everything in moderation” that defers
to industry interests.
Given this history, the wide range of foods to be avoided or lim￾ited in the newDGAs is remarkable.It includes not only sugary drinks,
but also chips, cookies, candy, white bread, packaged breakfast ce￾reals, crackers,meatswith chemicaladditives (like nitrites),andmore.
The update further advises, for the first time, limiting products with
artificial flavors, petroleum-based dyes, artificial preservatives, or
nonnutritive sweeteners. Limits on added sugar are also strength￾ened per product, per meal, and by age group, including new guid￾ance for zero intake of added sugar from birth through 10 years of
age.In sum, theDGAs advise against60% to70% of the current food
supply,3 a landmark change from prior iterations and an unmistak￾able signal to the food industry.
Encouraging More Whole Foods
A second positive update is the major focus on whole or minimally
processed foods, fiber-richwhole grains, and healthy fats. PriorDGAs
have included similar points, but not with the same emphasis. De￾ficiencies in these foods contribute to much of the chronic disease
burden in theUS.A relatedmajor change is thatwhole-fat dairy foods
with no added sugars can be included, which is consistent with the
accumulated evidence of no meaningful benefit in choosing low￾fat dairy over whole-fat dairy.2,4 When combined with new guid￾ance on highly processed foods, added sugars, artificial sweeten￾ers, and other additives—encapsulated in a new tagline, “eat real
food”—these changes could transform meals and snacks for chil￾dren (eg, away from flavored, low-fat milks or yogurts toward plain
whole-fat options and away from sweetened refined grain snacks
toward healthy oils and whole grains).
A shortcoming is insufficient nuance on the hierarchy of fat
sources. Plant, dairy, and animal sources are grouped together,
belying the evidence that plant and seafood sources provide the
greatest benefits, followed by dairy (especially fermented options
like yogurt or cheese), and that red and processed meats are less
salubrious, less due to their fat than other carcinogenic and pro￾inflammatory compounds.5 The DGAs mention butter and beef
tallow as options, but on a positive note recommend prioritizing
“oils with essential fatty acids, such as olive oil”1
and do not advise
against omega-6 fats or seed oils, which are oils that have been dis￾paraged in social media campaigns despite their well-established
health benefits.5
A Boost to Protein
A third major change is that the DGAs recommended higher di￾etary protein from the existing Dietary Reference Intake of 0.8 g/kg
of body weight per day to a target of 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg of body weight
per day. For an average adult, this change translates to approxi￾mately 16% to 21% of calories from protein, which is higher than
the current national average intake of 16%.6 Although dietary pro￾tein can increase muscle mass and strength when combined with
regular strength or resistance training, there is little evidence
that, absent sustained training, higher protein builds muscle or pro￾vides other health benefits.7,8 In fact, excess dietary protein can be
converted to fat by the liver, increasing visceral adiposity and dia￾betes risk.8,9

the Department of Defense) requires rulemaking and policy change

needed to produce healthy food that is widely accessible and
affordable.
Accordingly, it will be critical to follow how robustly the DGAs
will be communicated to the public, incorporated into agency policy,

Dariush Mozaffarian, MD, DrPH
On January 7, 2026,the US Department of Health and Human Ser￾vices and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) released the
2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGAs),1
which by law
are revised every 5 years. Interest in this update has been height￾ened by the Trump administration’s focus on food and health, prior
provocative statements on nutrition, departures from usual admin￾istrative and scientific processes in other areas (eg, vaccines), and
the Make America Healthy Again movement.
TheDGAs serve as the nation’s nutritional recommendations for
the general population and directly inform procurement standards
in schools and day-care facilities, other federal nutrition programs,
military nutrition, and federal cafeterias. The DGAs also influence in￾dustry formulationsandmarketing.A clear understanding of the con￾tents of the DGAs, their implications, and unanswered questions is
critical for those interested in patient care, public health, scientific
research, and policy.
First-Ever Limits on Processed Foods
Several updates to the DGAs1
are salient (Table). The most notable is
a major emphasis on limiting or avoiding foods that are highly pro￾cessed, packaged, or ready toeat; sugar-sweetened beverages; other
foods high in added sugars or sodium; and refined, highly processed
carbohydrates. These foods are consistently associated with ad￾verse health outcomes and arewidely overconsumed; refined grains,
for example, are themost problematic of this group and are overcon￾sumed by more than 95% of individuals in the US.2Yet, even though
groups such as the American Heart Association and prior indepen￾dent Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committees have advised against
such foods, no prior DGAs carried forward such recommendations.
Previously, the government appeared unwilling or unable to make
statements that might threaten sales of any particular food sector.
Instead, prior DGAs generally presented all food choices as ac￾ceptablewithin certain daily nutrient targets, such as for salt or sugar.
This implicitly permitted foods like soda and processedmeats within
a healthful pattern, provided that overall nutrient targets were
met—an approach inconsistent with evidence for harms of certain
products. In schoolmeals, for example, highly processed items such
as flavoredmilks, refined-grain entrées, processedmeats, and pack￾aged snack foods are permitted even though these do not pro￾mote optimal health.With this approach, there are no “bad foods”—a
strategy for nourishment of “everything in moderation” that defers
to industry interests.
Given this history, the wide range of foods to be avoided or lim￾ited in the newDGAs is remarkable.It includes not only sugary drinks,
but also chips, cookies, candy, white bread, packaged breakfast ce￾reals, crackers,meatswith chemicaladditives (like nitrites),andmore.
The update further advises, for the first time, limiting products with
artificial flavors, petroleum-based dyes, artificial preservatives, or
nonnutritive sweeteners. Limits on added sugar are also strength￾ened per product, per meal, and by age group, including new guid￾ance for zero intake of added sugar from birth through 10 years of
age.In sum, theDGAs advise against60% to70% of the current food
supply,3 a landmark change from prior iterations and an unmistak￾able signal to the food industry.
Encouraging More Whole Foods
A second positive update is the major focus on whole or minimally
processed foods, fiber-richwhole grains, and healthy fats. PriorDGAs
have included similar points, but not with the same emphasis. De￾ficiencies in these foods contribute to much of the chronic disease
burden in theUS.A relatedmajor change is thatwhole-fat dairy foods
with no added sugars can be included, which is consistent with the
accumulated evidence of no meaningful benefit in choosing low￾fat dairy over whole-fat dairy.2,4 When combined with new guid￾ance on highly processed foods, added sugars, artificial sweeten￾ers, and other additives—encapsulated in a new tagline, “eat real
food”—these changes could transform meals and snacks for chil￾dren (eg, away from flavored, low-fat milks or yogurts toward plain
whole-fat options and away from sweetened refined grain snacks
toward healthy oils and whole grains).
A shortcoming is insufficient nuance on the hierarchy of fat
sources. Plant, dairy, and animal sources are grouped together,
belying the evidence that plant and seafood sources provide the
greatest benefits, followed by dairy (especially fermented options
like yogurt or cheese), and that red and processed meats are less
salubrious, less due to their fat than other carcinogenic and pro￾inflammatory compounds.5 The DGAs mention butter and beef
tallow as options, but on a positive note recommend prioritizing
“oils with essential fatty acids, such as olive oil”1
and do not advise
against omega-6 fats or seed oils, which are oils that have been dis￾paraged in social media campaigns despite their well-established
health benefits.5

A third major change is that the DGAs recommended higher di￾etary protein from the existing Dietary Reference Intake of 0.8 g/kg
of body weight per day to a target of 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg of body weight
per day. For an average adult, this change translates to approxi￾mately 16% to 21% of calories from protein, which is higher than
the current national average intake of 16%.6 Although dietary pro￾tein can increase muscle mass and strength when combined with
regular strength or resistance training, there is little evidence
that, absent sustained training, higher protein builds muscle or pro￾vides other health benefits.7,8 In fact, excess dietary protein can be
converted to fat by the liver, increasing visceral adiposity and dia￾betes risk.8,9

* The 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans
Dariush Mozaffarian, MD, DrPH
On January 7, 2026,the US Department of Health and Human Ser￾vices and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) released the
2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGAs),1
which by law
are revised every 5 years. Interest in this update has been height￾ened by the Trump administration’s focus on food and health, prior
provocative statements on nutrition, departures from usual admin￾istrative and scientific processes in other areas (eg, vaccines), and
the Make America Healthy Again movement.
TheDGAs serve as the nation’s nutritional recommendations for
the general population and directly inform procurement standards
in schools and day-care facilities, other federal nutrition programs,
military nutrition, and federal cafeterias. The DGAs also influence in￾dustry formulationsandmarketing.A clear understanding of the con￾tents of the DGAs, their implications, and unanswered questions is
critical for those interested in patient care, public health, scientific
research, and policy.
First-Ever Limits on Processed Foods
Several updates to the DGAs1
are salient (Table). The most notable is
a major emphasis on limiting or avoiding foods that are highly pro￾cessed, packaged, or ready toeat; sugar-sweetened beverages; other
foods high in added sugars or sodium; and refined, highly processed
carbohydrates. These foods are consistently associated with ad￾verse health outcomes and arewidely overconsumed; refined grains,
for example, are themost problematic of this group and are overcon￾sumed by more than 95% of individuals in the US.2Yet, even though
groups such as the American Heart Association and prior indepen￾dent Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committees have advised against
such foods, no prior DGAs carried forward such recommendations.
Previously, the government appeared unwilling or unable to make
statements that might threaten sales of any particular food sector.
Instead, prior DGAs generally presented all food choices as ac￾ceptablewithin certain daily nutrient targets, such as for salt or sugar.
This implicitly permitted foods like soda and processedmeats within
a healthful pattern, provided that overall nutrient targets were
met—an approach inconsistent with evidence for harms of certain
products. In schoolmeals, for example, highly processed items such
as flavoredmilks, refined-grain entrées, processedmeats, and pack￾aged snack foods are permitted even though these do not pro￾mote optimal health.With this approach, there are no “bad foods”—a
strategy for nourishment of “everything in moderation” that defers
to industry interests.
Given this history, the wide range of foods to be avoided or lim￾ited in the newDGAs is remarkable.It includes not only sugary drinks,
but also chips, cookies, candy, white bread, packaged breakfast ce￾reals, crackers,meatswith chemicaladditives (like nitrites),andmore.
The update further advises, for the first time, limiting products with
artificial flavors, petroleum-based dyes, artificial preservatives, or
nonnutritive sweeteners. Limits on added sugar are also strength￾ened per product, per meal, and by age group, including new guid￾ance for zero intake of added sugar from birth through 10 years of
age.In sum, theDGAs advise against60% to70% of the current food
supply,3 a landmark change from prior iterations and an unmistak￾able signal to the food industry.
Encouraging More Whole Foods
A second positive update is the major focus on whole or minimally
processed foods, fiber-richwhole grains, and healthy fats. PriorDGAs
have included similar points, but not with the same emphasis. De￾ficiencies in these foods contribute to much of the chronic disease
burden in theUS.A relatedmajor change is thatwhole-fat dairy foods
with no added sugars can be included, which is consistent with the
accumulated evidence of no meaningful benefit in choosing low￾fat dairy over whole-fat dairy.2,4 When combined with new guid￾ance on highly processed foods, added sugars, artificial sweeten￾ers, and other additives—encapsulated in a new tagline, “eat real
food”—these changes could transform meals and snacks for chil￾dren (eg, away from flavored, low-fat milks or yogurts toward plain
whole-fat options and away from sweetened refined grain snacks
toward healthy oils and whole grains).
A shortcoming is insufficient nuance on the hierarchy of fat
sources. Plant, dairy, and animal sources are grouped together,
belying the evidence that plant and seafood sources provide the
greatest benefits, followed by dairy (especially fermented options
like yogurt or cheese), and that red and processed meats are less
salubrious, less due to their fat than other carcinogenic and pro￾inflammatory compounds.5 The DGAs mention butter and beef
tallow as options, but on a positive note recommend prioritizing
“oils with essential fatty acids, such as olive oil”1
and do not advise
against omega-6 fats or seed oils, which are oils that have been dis￾paraged in social media campaigns despite their well-established
health benefits.5
A Boost to Protein
A third major change is that the DGAs recommended higher di￾etary protein from the existing Dietary Reference Intake of 0.8 g/kg
of body weight per day to a target of 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg of body weight
per day. For an average adult, this change translates to approxi￾mately 16% to 21% of calories from protein, which is higher than
the current national average intake of 16%.6 Although dietary pro￾tein can increase muscle mass and strength when combined with
regular strength or resistance training, there is little evidence
that, absent sustained training, higher protein builds muscle or pro￾vides other health benefits.7,8 In fact, excess dietary protein can be
converted to fat by the liver, increasing visceral adiposity and dia￾betes risk.8,9

* The 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans
Dariush Mozaffarian, MD, DrPH
On January 7, 2026,the US Department of Health and Human Ser￾vices and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) released the
2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGAs),1
which by law
are revised every 5 years. Interest in this update has been height￾ened by the Trump administration’s focus on food and health, prior
provocative statements on nutrition, departures from usual admin￾istrative and scientific processes in other areas (eg, vaccines), and
the Make America Healthy Again movement.
TheDGAs serve as the nation’s nutritional recommendations for
the general population and directly inform procurement standards
in schools and day-care facilities, other federal nutrition programs,
military nutrition, and federal cafeterias. The DGAs also influence in￾dustry formulationsandmarketing.A clear understanding of the con￾tents of the DGAs, their implications, and unanswered questions is
critical for those interested in patient care, public health, scientific
research, and policy.
First-Ever Limits on Processed Foods
Several updates to the DGAs1
are salient (Table). The most notable is
a major emphasis on limiting or avoiding foods that are highly pro￾cessed, packaged, or ready toeat; sugar-sweetened beverages; other
foods high in added sugars or sodium; and refined, highly processed
carbohydrates. These foods are consistently associated with ad￾verse health outcomes and arewidely overconsumed; refined grains,
for example, are themost problematic of this group and are overcon￾sumed by more than 95% of individuals in the US.2Yet, even though
groups such as the American Heart Association and prior indepen￾dent Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committees have advised against
such foods, no prior DGAs carried forward such recommendations.
Previously, the government appeared unwilling or unable to make
statements that might threaten sales of any particular food sector.
Instead, prior DGAs generally presented all food choices as ac￾ceptablewithin certain daily nutrient targets, such as for salt or sugar.
This implicitly permitted foods like soda and processedmeats within
a healthful pattern, provided that overall nutrient targets were
met—an approach inconsistent with evidence for harms of certain
products. In schoolmeals, for example, highly processed items such
as flavoredmilks, refined-grain entrées, processedmeats, and pack￾aged snack foods are permitted even though these do not pro￾mote optimal health.With this approach, there are no “bad foods”—a
strategy for nourishment of “everything in moderation” that defers
to industry interests.
Given this history, the wide range of foods to be avoided or lim￾ited in the newDGAs is remarkable.It includes not only sugary drinks,
but also chips, cookies, candy, white bread, packaged breakfast ce￾reals, crackers,meatswith chemicaladditives (like nitrites),andmore.
The update further advises, for the first time, limiting products with
artificial flavors, petroleum-based dyes, artificial preservatives, or
nonnutritive sweeteners. Limits on added sugar are also strength￾ened per product, per meal, and by age group, including new guid￾ance for zero intake of added sugar from birth through 10 years of
age.In sum, theDGAs advise against60% to70% of the current food
supply,3 a landmark change from prior iterations and an unmistak￾able signal to the food industry.
Encouraging More Whole Foods
A second positive update is the major focus on whole or minimally
processed foods, fiber-richwhole grains, and healthy fats. PriorDGAs
have included similar points, but not with the same emphasis. De￾ficiencies in these foods contribute to much of the chronic disease
burden in theUS.A relatedmajor change is thatwhole-fat dairy foods
with no added sugars can be included, which is consistent with the
accumulated evidence of no meaningful benefit in choosing low￾fat dairy over whole-fat dairy.2,4 When combined with new guid￾ance on highly processed foods, added sugars, artificial sweeten￾ers, and other additives—encapsulated in a new tagline, “eat real
food”—these changes could transform meals and snacks for chil￾dren (eg, away from flavored, low-fat milks or yogurts toward plain
whole-fat options and away from sweetened refined grain snacks
toward healthy oils and whole grains).
A shortcoming is insufficient nuance on the hierarchy of fat
sources. Plant, dairy, and animal sources are grouped together,
belying the evidence that plant and seafood sources provide the
greatest benefits, followed by dairy (especially fermented options
like yogurt or cheese), and that red and processed meats are less
salubrious, less due to their fat than other carcinogenic and pro￾inflammatory compounds.5 The DGAs mention butter and beef
tallow as options, but on a positive note recommend prioritizing
“oils with essential fatty acids, such as olive oil”1
and do not advise
against omega-6 fats or seed oils, which are oils that have been dis￾paraged in social media campaigns despite their well-established
health benefits.5
A Boost to Protein
A third major change is that the DGAs recommended higher di￾etary protein from the existing Dietary Reference Intake of 0.8 g/kg
of body weight per day to a target of 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg of body weight
per day. For an average adult, this change translates to approxi￾mately 16% to 21% of calories from protein, which is higher than
the current national average intake of 16%.6 Although dietary pro￾tein can increase muscle mass and strength when combined with
regular strength or resistance training, there is little evidence
that, absent sustained training, higher protein builds muscle or pro￾vides other health benefits.7,8 In fact, excess dietary protein can be
converted to fat by the liver, increasing visceral adiposity and dia￾betes risk.8,9

question: How will the latest DGAs be put into practice? The DGAs

Operationalizing the DGAs in the agencies (from the USDA to
the Department of Defense) requires rulemaking and policy change
that can take years ormay never be fully realized. Executing changes
in schools, childcare, and cafeterias may require new funding and
technical support for which political support remains uncertain. In￾tegration of nutrition into clinical care necessitates reforms in medi￾cal education and health system payments. Changes to support and
creation of infrastructure for farms and small businesses will be
needed to produce healthy food that is widely accessible and
affordable.
Accordingly, it will be critical to follow how robustly the DGAs
will be communicated to the public, incorporated into agency policy,
and implemented in the community—steps that are essential to
achieving positive effects.

parts:
Yes — there are several strong iOS apps that combine **recipe storage + meal planning + grocery/shopping lists**, and we can plug our gourmet meal-plan recipes into them. I created a companion import pack with **Mela**, **Paprika YAML**, **Schema.org recipe pages**, **JSON-LD**, **CSV**, and **Markdown** exports:

[Download the recipe app import pack](sandbox:/mnt/data/recipe_app_import_pack.zip)

The pack preserves the metric measurements, mise en place, method steps, food-science notes, plating/pairing notes, and DGA-review metadata from the current project. The DGA layer matters because the uploaded PDF emphasizes avoiding ultra-processed foods, sugar-sweetened beverages, refined carbohydrates, and artificial additives while prioritizing whole/minimally processed foods, fiber-rich whole grains, healthy fats, and protein variety. fileciteturn0file0

## Best recommendation for our project

**Best practical choice: Paprika Recipe Manager 3.** It has recipes, grocery lists, pantry tracking, meal planning calendars, scaling, metric conversion, printing, offline access, and direct import support. Most importantly for us, Paprika documents a plain **YAML multi-recipe import format**, so our recipes can be loaded without needing to host each recipe as a webpage. citeturn608273search1turn832859view0

**Best Apple-native/premium UI choice: Mela.** Mela has iCloud sync, a beautiful cook mode, groceries stored in Apple Reminders, calendar-based meal planning, web import, scan import, and a documented `.melarecipe` / `.melarecipes` JSON format. I generated a ready-to-import `.melarecipes` file for it. citeturn501671search1turn940104view0

**Best shared grocery-list choice: AnyList.** AnyList is excellent for household shopping lists and can import recipes from websites using its iOS share extension; it explicitly says recipe import works from websites that support Schema.org microdata, so the Schema.org HTML pages in the import pack are the right route. citeturn762570search3turn762570search8

## Comparison of the strongest iOS options

| App | Best for | Recipe import | Shopping list | Meal planning | Fit for our recipes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Paprika Recipe Manager 3** | Power users, offline archive, serious meal planning | Web import, many app formats, `.yml`, `.paprikarecipes` | Smart grocery lists, aisle sorting, pantry | Daily/weekly/monthly calendar, reusable menus | **Excellent. Use the generated Paprika YAML file.** |
| **Mela** | Premium Apple-native experience | Web, scan, share extension, documented `.melarecipe` JSON | Uses Apple Reminders | Uses Calendar app / built-in calendar | **Excellent. Use the generated `.melarecipes` file.** |
| **AnyList** | Shared household grocery lists | Web import via iOS action extension; Schema.org-supported sites | Excellent shared lists, grocery categories | Calendar/list meal planning in Complete | **Very good. Use hosted Schema.org recipe pages.** |
| **Recipe Keeper** | Simple all-in-one, scanning old recipes | Web import, copy/paste, OCR from photos/PDFs, imports from many apps | Auto-grouped shopping list | Weekly/monthly meal planner | **Very good, especially through web pages or copy/paste.** citeturn948191search1 |
| **Crouton** | Modern guided cooking, Apple ecosystem | Web import, AI/OCR/photo/PDF import | Recipe-based shopping lists, Reminders integration | Weekly/future meal planning | **Very good, especially via Schema.org pages or AI import.** citeturn948191search0 |
| **Pestle** | Guided cooking and social/video recipe saving | Web import, TikTok/Instagram, scanner, imports Paprika/Crouton/Mela/Pepperplate | Ingredient-to-shopping-list workflow | 14-day meal planning and household sync | **Very good; can likely ingest Mela/Paprika route or web pages.** citeturn375206search0 |
| **MealBoard** | Pantry + grocery + meal planning | Web import, scanning, manual recipes | Aggregated list, stores, prices, pantry movement | Day/meal-type plans, templates, prep notifications | **Very strong for pantry operations.** citeturn948191search2 |
| **Samsung Food** | Free recipe discovery + nutrition + community | Save any recipe from any website | Shared grocery lists, retailer integrations in some regions | Weekly meal planning, AI plans in paid tier | **Good, but less ideal for preserving our custom notes.** citeturn985532search0 |
| **CookBook** | AI-heavy import and macro tracking | Websites, social apps, scanner, AI recipe tools | Smart aisle-sorted list, sync | Day/week/month planner | **Good for AI import, less transparent for bulk migration.** citeturn985532search4 |
| **Umami** | Clean collaborative recipe books | Browser import, URL paste, web app; exports PDF/Markdown/HTML/Text/Recipe JSON Schema | Shared grocery lists, by aisle or recipe | Calendar meal plans | **Promising; best route is hosted Schema.org or manual import.** citeturn985532search2 |

## Best import route for our recipes

### 1. Paprika direct import — most reliable for bulk loading

Use this file from the import pack:

```text
recipe_app_import_pack/paprika/gourmet-meal-plan-paprika.yml
```

Paprika’s iOS guide says it can import `.yml` recipe files and documents a multi-recipe YAML structure with `name`, `servings`, `prep_time`, `cook_time`, `categories`, `notes`, `ingredients`, and `directions`. citeturn832859view0

Our generated YAML maps the plan like this:

| Our field | Paprika field |
|---|---|
| Recipe name | `name` |
| Servings | `servings` |
| Active time | `prep_time` |
| Total time | `cook_time` |
| Cuisine + meal type + DGA reviewed | `categories` |
| Ingredient groups | `ingredients` |
| Mise en place + method steps | `directions` |
| Why this works + plating/pairing + DGA notes | `notes` |

### 2. Mela direct import — best Apple-native route

Use this file:

```text
recipe_app_import_pack/mela/gourmet-meal-plan-dga-reviewed.melarecipes
```

Mela documents `.melarecipes` as a ZIP of `.melarecipe` JSON files, and each recipe supports fields like title, text, categories, yield, prep time, total time, ingredients, instructions, notes, nutrition, and link. citeturn940104view0

Our mapping:

| Our field | Mela field |
|---|---|
| Recipe name | `title` |
| Cuisine/summary | `text` |
| Cuisine + meal type + DGA reviewed | `categories` |
| Servings | `yield` |
| Active time | `prepTime` |
| Total time | `totalTime` |
| Ingredient groups | `ingredients` |
| Mise en place + method steps | `instructions` |
| Why this works + plating/pairing + DGA notes | `notes` |

### 3. Universal web-import route — best for AnyList, Recipe Keeper, Crouton, Samsung Food, CookBook, MealBoard

Use this folder:

```text
recipe_app_import_pack/schema-org-html/
```

Deploy it to GitHub Pages or any static host, then open each recipe page in Safari and use the app’s share/import extension. AnyList explicitly says it can import recipes from websites that support Schema.org microdata, and Schema.org’s `Recipe` type supports fields like `recipeIngredient`, `recipeInstructions`, `prepTime`, `cookTime`, `totalTime`, `recipeYield`, and `recipeCuisine`. citeturn762570search8turn912647search1

This route is also safer for apps that do not expose a bulk-file import format. The tradeoff is that some apps may import only the standard recipe fields and place our “why this works,” pairing, and DGA notes into descriptions/notes rather than preserving them as custom sections.

## What I generated

The import pack contains:

```text
recipe_app_import_pack/
├── README_IMPORT_OPTIONS.md
├── APP_RESEARCH_SUMMARY.md
├── mela/
│   ├── gourmet-meal-plan-dga-reviewed.melarecipes
│   └── individual_melarecipe_files/
├── paprika/
│   └── gourmet-meal-plan-paprika.yml
├── schema-org-html/
│   ├── index.html
│   └── recipes/*.html
├── schema-org-jsonld/
│   ├── recipes-schemaorg-graph.jsonld
│   └── one JSON-LD file per recipe
├── csv/
│   ├── recipes.csv
│   └── shopping_lists.csv
└── markdown/
    ├── recipes.md
    └── shopping-lists.md
```

## Practical recommendation

Use **Paprika** if the goal is maximum reliability, pantry/shopping/meal planning depth, and one-file import. Use **Mela** if the goal is the nicest Apple-native experience with Reminders and Calendar integration. Use **AnyList** if the priority is shared family grocery shopping, but import the recipes through the hosted Schema.org pages rather than expecting perfect bulk import.

For our current GitHub SPA, the best next step is to add the import pack as an `/exports/` folder and link it from the README so the project supports both: a beautiful custom web app and migration into mainstream recipe apps.

**Cuisines & Cultural Inspirations**
- **Peruvian/Nikkei:** Frequent orders of artichoke empanadas, quinua bowls, Inca‑inspired drinks, maki acevichado and takoyaki show a love of Peru’s Nikkei fusion and seafood‑driven dishes.

# 1. Executive Summary

This one‑month gourmet plan synthesises the new 2025–2030 dietary guidelines with the user’s demonstrated tastes. Each recipe in this plan uses whole‑grain bases, fresh produce, full‑fat dairy without added sugar, and homemade sauces to meet those standards. Over four themed weeks—Peruvian‑Nikkei & seafood, Italian‑Mediterranean, Mexican & Asian street food, and elevated American comfort—the user journeys through familiar flavours elevated to Michelin‑level sophistication. **Theme:** Introduce the month with dishes that celebrate Peru’s Nikkei heritage and the user’s love of eggs, artichokes and seafood. Expect bright citrus and ají sauces balancing creamy elements.

- Early prep: make whole‑grain English muffins and croissant dough; prepare fish stock and roast purple corn for dessert syrup.

## Week 2 – Italian & Mediterranean Comfort
**Theme:** Honour Italian classics—pasta, pizza, risotto—reimagined with whole grains and Peruvian accents. Rich cheeses and sauces pair with roasted vegetables and seafood.

**Highlights:**
- Brown rice risotto, whole‑grain gnocchi and pizza dough highlight fibre‑rich grains.
- Parmesan, pecorino and mozzarella used judiciously to add umami without overwhelming.
- Artichokes, mushrooms, tomatoes and olives provide plant variety; herbs like basil, oregano and rosemary.
- Prep tasks include fermenting pizza dough overnight, soaking brown rice, and making lucuma purée for tiramisu.

## Week 3 – Mexican & Asian Street Food Remix
**Theme:** A playful mash‑up of Mexican street dishes and East Asian favourites, featuring tacos, ramen and mapo tofu. Spices, fermented flavours and pickles keep dishes lively.

**Highlights:**
- Whole‑grain tortillas, brown rice and quinoa support tacos and bowls.
- Homemade salsas (salsa roja, chipotle crema), miso glazes and birria broth provide depth.
- Proteins include sustainable fish, miso‑glazed salmon, slow‑braised lamb or beef, turkey mince and tofu.
- Prepare birria base and ramen broth ahead; ferment kimchi and prepare churro dough a day prior.

## Week 4 – Elevated American Classics
**Theme:** Finish with comfort foods elevated through technique—sous‑vide short ribs, gourmet burgers and refined fried chicken. Sweet dishes showcase balanced indulgence.

**Highlights:**
- Whole‑grain bagels and sourdough for breakfast; almond‑flour breading for fried chicken; farro and purple potatoes for starch.
- Focus on searing and sous‑vide for perfect textures and controlled fat content.
- Desserts like whiskey‑pecan tart use dark chocolate and nuts to satisfy sweet cravings while limiting added sugar.
- Prep includes curing salmon for bagels, marinating chicken and ribs, and making truffle salt for popcorn.

# 3. Daily Meal Plans

### Week 1 Daily Plan

| Day | Breakfast | Lunch | Dinner | Snack/Dessert |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Mon** | Artichoke Benedict with Trout | Nikkei Quinoa Acevichado Salad | Whole‑Grain Gnocchi a la Huancaína | Dark Chocolate & Chicha Morada Mousse |
| **Tue** | Takoyaki‑Inspired Omelette Roll | Chifa Lomo Saltado Quinoa Bowl | Deconstructed Acevichado Cod | Roasted Plantain Chips with Rocoto Dip |

Lo siento por la confusión, pero en este momento no puedo conectarme a Internet para investigar recetas. Sin embargo, he utilizado los datos de la conversación anterior y mi conocimiento para crear un conjunto de recetas adaptadas a Instant Pot, cumpliendo con tus especificaciones de recetas saludables y con las directrices alimentarias vigentes【32402232832100†L130-L179】.

### ✅ Resumen

Se adaptaron **6 recetas** porque aportan variedad de sabores y texturas, aprovechan la función de cocción a presión de la Instant Pot, utilizan proteínas de calidad y granos integrales, y se ajustan a las pautas nutricionales (evitando ultraprocesados y limitando azúcares añadidos)【32402232832100†L130-L179】. Cada receta fue revisada y ajustada para respetar las proporciones de macronutrientes, minimizar el sodio y las grasas saturadas, y potenciar sabores con especias naturales.

---

### 🍲 Recetas adaptadas

#### 1. Chili de Quinoa y Frijoles Negros — *Chili de Quinoa y Frijoles Andes*

- **Nombre original**: Instant Pot Black Bean & Quinoa Chili  
  **Nombre adaptado**: Chili de Quinoa y Frijoles Andes
- **Tiempo total**: 45 min (15 min preparación + 30 min cocción).  
  **Porciones**: 4–6.
- **Ingredientes**:
  - 250 g de frijoles negros secos (remojados 8 h y escurridos)  
  - 150 g de quinoa tricolor, lavada  
  - 1 cebolla roja (150 g) picada finamente  
  - 2 dientes de ajo (5 g) picados  
  - 1 pimiento rojo (120 g) en dados  
  - 1 zanahoria (80 g) rallada  
  - 400 g de tomate triturado sin sal añadida  
  - 800 ml de caldo de verduras bajo en sodio  
  - 15 ml de aceite de oliva virgen extra  
  - 10 g de chile en polvo  
  - 5 g de comino molido  
  - 5 g de orégano seco  
  - 3 g de paprika ahumada  
  - Sal marina y pimienta al gusto
  - Opcional: 20 g de cilantro fresco picado, 1 limón en gajos.
- **Instrucciones (Instant Pot)**:
  1. Selecciona la función *Sauté* y calienta el aceite. Añade la cebolla y el pimiento, sofríe 3 min hasta que estén ligeramente dorados.  
  2. Incorpora el ajo y la zanahoria, cocina 1 min. Agrega el chile en polvo, comino, orégano y paprika; mezcla para tostar especias 30 seg.  
  3. Añade frijoles remojados, quinoa, tomate triturado y caldo de verduras. Remueve y raspa el fondo para evitar que se pegue.  
  4. Cierra la tapa, verifica que la válvula esté en “Sell”. Selecciona *Pressure Cook* (alto) 25 min.  
  5. Al finalizar, deja liberar presión naturalmente 10 min, luego activa la liberación rápida.  
  6. Destapa, ajusta sal/pimienta. Si deseas una textura más espesa, activa *Sauté* y reduce 5 min.  
  7. Sirve con cilantro y gajos de limón para aportar frescor.
- **Notas de adaptación**:
  - Se sustituyeron frijoles enlatados por frijoles secos remojados para evitar conservadores y sodio【32402232832100†L130-L179】.
  - La quinoa aporta proteína vegetal y fibra.  
  - Las especias incrementan el sabor sin recurrir a salsas procesadas.

---

#### 2. Pollo Tikka Masala con Arroz Integral — *Pollo Tikka Masala Andino*

- **Nombre original**: Instant Pot Chicken Tikka Masala with Rice  
  **Nombre adaptado**: Pollo Tikka Masala Andino
- **Tiempo total**: 50 min (20 min preparación + 30 min cocción).  
  **Porciones**: 4.
- **Ingredientes**:
  - 600 g de pechuga de pollo sin piel, cortada en cubos de 3 cm  
  - 200 g de arroz integral de grano largo, enjuagado  
  - 1 cebolla blanca (120 g) picada  
  - 3 dientes de ajo (8 g) picados  
  - 15 g de jengibre fresco rallado  
  - 400 g de tomate triturado sin sal añadida  
  - 400 ml de leche de coco ligera (sin aditivos)  
  - 200 ml de caldo de pollo bajo en sodio  
  - 15 ml de aceite de oliva  
  - 5 g de garam masala  
  - 5 g de cúrcuma molida  
  - 5 g de comino molido  
  - 5 g de pimentón dulce  
  - 2 g de chile en hojuelas (ajustar picante)  
  - 50 g de yogur natural descremado  
  - Sal y pimienta.
- **Instrucciones**:
  1. Selecciona *Sauté* y calienta el aceite. Añade cebolla y saltea 3 min. Incorpora ajo y jengibre; cocina 1 min.  
  2. Agrega garam masala, cúrcuma, comino, pimentón y chile. Mezcla para tostar 30 seg.  
  3. Añade pollo, sazona con sal/pimienta, dora 2 min removiendo.  
  4. Incorpora tomate triturado, leche de coco y caldo; mezcla bien.  
  5. Sobre la mezcla, coloca una rejilla o cestillo interior y añade el arroz integral con 300 ml de agua. Asegura que el arroz no toque el líquido del pollo.  
  6. Cierra la tapa, válvula en “Sell”, selecciona *Pressure Cook* (alto) 10 min.  
  7. Cuando termine, libera presión naturalmente 10 min y luego ventila. Retira el cestillo, suelta el arroz con tenedor.  
  8. Añade yogur al curry y remueve en modo *Sauté* 2 min sin hervir. Ajusta sal.  
  9. Sirve el curry sobre arroz integral.
- **Notas de adaptación**:
  - Se usa leche de coco ligera sin azúcar y yogur descremado para reducir grasa saturada.  
  - La cocción en rejilla permite preparar arroz integral simultáneamente sin que se sobrecocine.  
  - Se evita uso de pastas comerciales y se incorpora mezcla de especias caseras y tomate natural【32402232832100†L130-L179】.

---

#### 3. Estofado de Res y Vegetales con Cebada — *Guiso Andino de Res y Cebada*

- **Nombre original**: Instant Pot Beef Stew with Barley  
  **Nombre adaptado**: Guiso Andino de Res y Cebada
- **Tiempo total**: 1 h 15 min (20 min preparación + 55 min cocción).  
  **Porciones**: 6.
- **Ingredientes**:
  - 700 g de carne magra de res (aguja o paleta), en cubos de 3 cm  
  - 120 g de cebada perlada integral, enjuagada  
  - 1 cebolla amarilla (150 g) picada  
  - 2 tallos de apio (100 g) en rodajas  
  - 2 zanahorias (160 g) en cubos  
  - 2 papas amarillas (300 g) en cubos  
  - 2 dientes de ajo (5 g) picados  
  - 30 g de pasta de tomate sin sal ni azúcar  
  - 750 ml de caldo de res bajo en sodio  
  - 5 ml de salsa de soja baja en sodio  
  - 5 ml de aceite de oliva  
  - 2 g de tomillo seco  
  - 2 g de romero seco  
  - 1 hoja de laurel  
  - Sal y pimienta.
- **Instrucciones**:
  1. Selecciona *Sauté* en la Instant Pot, agrega aceite y dora la carne por tandas (5 min). Reserva.  
  2. En el mismo recipiente, sofríe cebolla, apio y zanahoria 3 min. Añade ajo y pasta de tomate, cocina 1 min.  
  3. Vuelve a añadir la carne y agrega cebada, papas, caldo, salsa de soja, tomillo, romero y laurel. Desglasa el fondo.  
  4. Cierra la tapa, válvula en “Sell”. Programa *Pressure Cook* (alto) 30 min.  
  5. Liberación natural durante 15 min. Retira la hoja de laurel. Ajusta sal/pimienta.  
  6. Si deseas espesar, activa *Sauté* 5 min extra.  
  7. Sirve caliente con perejil picado.
- **Notas de adaptación**:
  - Se emplea carne magra y salsa de soja reducida en sodio para controlar grasas y sal.  
  - La cebada aporta fibra y modera la carga glucémica.  
  - Se elimina cualquier harina refinada; el espesado se logra por reducción natural【32402232832100†L130-L179】.

---

#### 4. Sopa de Lentejas Rojas y Verduras — *Sopa de Lentejas Andinas*

- **Nombre original**: Instant Pot Red Lentil Soup  
  **Nombre adaptado**: Sopa de Lentejas Andinas
- **Tiempo total**: 35 min (10 min preparación + 25 min cocción).  
  **Porciones**: 4–5.
- **Ingredientes**:
  - 300 g de lentejas rojas secas, enjuagadas  
  - 1 cebolla morada (100 g) picada  
  - 1 zanahoria (80 g) en cubos  
  - 1 rama de apio (50 g) picada  
  - 2 tomates (200 g) picados  
  - 1 litro de caldo de verduras bajo en sodio  
  - 15 ml de aceite de oliva  
  - 5 g de curry en polvo  
  - 2 g de cúrcuma  
  - 2 g de comino molido  
  - 1 g de pimienta negra  
  - Sal al gusto  
  - 1 L de agua adicional si es necesario  
  - Cilantro o perejil fresco para servir.
- **Instrucciones**:
  1. En modo *Sauté*, calienta el aceite y sofríe cebolla, zanahoria y apio 3 min.  
  2. Añade curry, cúrcuma, comino y pimienta. Tuesta 30 seg.  
  3. Incorpora tomates y cocina 2 min hasta que liberen jugos.  
  4. Agrega lentejas y caldo. Remueve.  
  5. Cierra la tapa, válvula en “Sell”. Selecciona *Pressure Cook* (alto) 8 min.  
  6. Realiza liberación rápida. Verifica consistencia; para una textura más cremosa, tritura con batidora de mano.  
  7. Ajusta sal y diluye con agua si queda demasiado espesa. Sirve con cilantro o perejil.
- **Notas de adaptación**:
  - Las lentejas rojas se cocinan rápidamente y proporcionan proteína vegetal y hierro.  
  - Las especias añaden sabor sin salsas procesadas ni exceso de sodio【32402232832100†L130-L179】.

---

#### 5. Salmón Teriyaki con Quinoa — *Salmón Nikkei en Instant Pot*

- **Nombre original**: Instant Pot Teriyaki Salmon with Quinoa  
  **Nombre adaptado**: Salmón Nikkei en Instant Pot
- **Tiempo total**: 25 min (10 min preparación + 15 min cocción).  
  **Porciones**: 4.
- **Ingredientes**:
  - 600 g de filetes de salmón sin piel, cortados en 4 porciones  
  - 150 g de quinoa blanca, lavada  
  - 375 ml de agua para la quinoa  
  - 30 ml de salsa de soja baja en sodio  
  - 20 ml de mirin sin azúcar añadido  
  - 20 ml de sake o vino de arroz (opcional, puede sustituirse por caldo)  
  - 15 ml de miel pura (≈10 g de azúcares añadidos en total)  
  - 10 ml de aceite de sésamo tostado  
  - 5 g de jengibre rallado  
  - 1 diente de ajo (3 g) picado  
  - 2 g de semillas de sésamo tostadas  
  - 20 g de cebollino picado  
  - 20 ml de agua para disolver la miel.
- **Instrucciones**:
  1. En un bol, mezcla salsa de soja, mirin, sake (o caldo), miel, jengibre y ajo para preparar la salsa teriyaki.  
  2. Vierte la quinoa y el agua en la cubeta de la Instant Pot. Coloca una rejilla metálica y sobre ella los filetes de salmón.  
  3. Cubre el salmón con la mitad de la salsa teriyaki. Reserva el resto.  
  4. Cierra la tapa, válvula en “Sell” y programa *Pressure Cook* (alto) 3 min.  
  5. Tras finalizar, espera 5 min y realiza liberación rápida. Retira el salmón.  
  6. Activa *Sauté*, incorpora la salsa restante con el jugo liberado; reduce 2–3 min hasta espesar ligeramente.  
  7. Desmenuza la quinoa con un tenedor. Sirve el salmón sobre la quinoa, baña con la salsa reducida y espolvorea semillas de sésamo y cebollino.
- **Notas de adaptación**:
  - Se usa salsa de soja reducida en sodio y miel en pequeña cantidad para no exceder 10 g de azúcar añadido por ración【32402232832100†L130-L179】.  
  - La quinoa absorbe el líquido, aportando textura y proteínas.  
  - El salmón es rico en omega 3 y encaja con las directrices de consumir grasas saludables.

---

#### 6. Avena Steel-Cut con Chía y Berries — *Avena Integral en Instant Pot*

- **Nombre original**: Instant Pot Steel-Cut Oats with Fruit  
  **Nombre adaptado**: Avena Integral en Instant Pot
- **Tiempo total**: 30 min (5 min preparación + 25 min cocción).  
  **Porciones**: 4.
- **Ingredientes**:
  - 200 g de avena steel-cut (cortes de acero)  
  - 800 ml de agua  
  - 250 ml de leche descremada o bebida vegetal sin azúcar  
  - 30 g de semillas de chía  
  - 100 g de arándanos frescos o congelados  
  - 100 g de fresas en cubos  
  - 10 ml de extracto de vainilla natural  
  - 5 g de canela molida  
  - 15 ml de jarabe de arce puro (contiene ≈9 g de azúcares añadidos repartidos en 4 porciones)  
  - Pizca de sal.
- **Instrucciones**:
  1. Coloca avena, agua, leche y sal en la cubeta. Remueve.  
  2. Cierra la tapa, válvula en “Sell”, selecciona *Pressure Cook* (alto) 4 min.  
  3. Al terminar, deja liberar presión naturalmente 15 min para evitar que salga espuma por la válvula.  
  4. Destapa, añade chía, vainilla y canela; mezcla y deja reposar 5 min para que espese.  
  5. Incorpora la mitad de los frutos rojos. Sirve en boles y decora con frutos restantes y un hilo de jarabe de arce.
- **Notas de adaptación**:
  - La avena steel-cut y la chía son fuentes de fibra soluble y proteínas vegetales.  
  - El jarabe de arce se dosifica para no superar 10 g de azúcar añadido【32402232832100†L130-L179】.  
  - Utiliza leche descremada o bebida vegetal sin azúcar para reducir grasas saturadas.

---

### 🛒 Lista de compras consolidada

| Categoría | Ingredientes (total) |
|---|---|
| **Verduras y hortalizas** | 3 cebollas (1 roja, 1 blanca, 1 amarilla), 4 zanahorias, 3 ramas de apio, 1 pimiento rojo, 2 tomates, 2 papas amarillas, 1 limón, 1 jengibre de 40 g, 1 ajo entero (varios dientes), cilantro o perejil, cebollino, 200 g de berries (arándanos y fresas). |
| **Legumbres y granos** | 250 g frijoles negros secos, 150 g quinoa tricolor + 150 g quinoa blanca, 120 g cebada integral, 300 g lentejas rojas, 200 g avena steel-cut, 200 g arroz integral, 30 g semillas de chía. |
| **Proteínas animales** | 600 g pechuga de pollo, 700 g carne magra de res, 600 g filetes de salmón, 1 L de leche descremada o bebida vegetal. |
| **Lácteos y alternativos** | 50 g yogur natural descremado. |
| **Líquidos y caldos** | 800 ml + 1 L de caldo de verduras bajo en sodio, 750 ml de caldo de res bajo en sodio, 200 ml de caldo de pollo bajo en sodio (para tikka masala), 400 ml leche de coco ligera. |
| **Especias y condimentos** | Aceite de oliva virgen extra (≈45 ml), aceite de sésamo tostado (10 ml), salsa de soja baja en sodio (35 ml), mirin (20 ml), sake o vino de arroz (20 ml opcional), miel pura (15 ml), jarabe de arce puro (15 ml), pasta de tomate (30 g), tomate triturado (800 g), garam masala (5 g), cúrcuma (7 g), comino (12 g), curry en polvo (5 g), paprika ahumada (3 g), pimentón dulce (5 g), orégano (5 g), tomillo (2 g), romero (2 g), hoja de laurel (1), chile en polvo y hojuelas (al gusto), extracto de vainilla (10 ml), semillas de sésamo (2 g), canela molida (5 g), sal marina y pimienta. |

> **Nota**: Esta lista consolida las cantidades de todas las recetas; ajusta según el número de porciones deseado. Las especias se compran en pequeñas cantidades, por lo que se indica un aproximado para cubrir las preparaciones.

---

Estas recetas y su lista de compras están cuidadosamente adaptadas para respetar las directrices dietéticas actuales, con un enfoque en ingredientes naturales, control de sodio y azúcares añadidos y mayor consumo de fibra y proteínas de calidad【32402232832100†L130-L179】. Espero que disfrutes de estas preparaciones en tu Instant Pot y que te faciliten el meal prep de forma saludable y deliciosa.

metadata.text: Recommendationsa Implications • Avoid foods that are highly processed, packaged, or ready to eat • Avoid other foods that are salty or sweet • Prior DGAs generally presented all food choices as acceptable within overall daily nutrient limits; an approach that was inconsistent with the evidence for harms of certain types of products • No prior DGA has emphasized the dimension of processing separately from nutrients or food groups • This update directly challenges widespread industry products and practices • Avoid sugar-sweetened beverages • Limit added sugars to no more than 10 g per meal and, in foods, to the US Food and Drug Administration healthy rule (eg, 5 g in grains, 2.5 g in dairy) • No added sugars from birth through 10 y of age • The 2010 DGA advised against sugar-sweetened beverages, but this recommendation was dropped in subsequent updates • The new recommendations for sugar-sweetened beverages and added sugars are much stronger than in prior editions • Limit foods and beverages that include artificial flavors, petroleum-based dyes, artificial preservatives, and low-calorie nonnutritive sweeteners • Although evidence on these additives remains limited and conflicting, emerging studies suggest potential adverse effects on glucose control, microbiome composition, child behavior, and other outcomes • No prior DGAs have recommended their avoidance; indeed, some prior DGA educational materials have promoted nonnutritive sweeteners as a sugar-reduction strategy • The impact will greatly depend on how this is communicated to the public and implemented in agency policy (eg, school meals, early childcare, military nutrition, federal cafeterias) • Prioritize fiber-rich whole grains • Significantly reduce highly processed, refined carbohydrates • No prior DGAs have recommended reducing processed or refined carbohydrates (eg, refined wheat, rice, or corn flour); prior DGAs only recommended to partly replace refined grains with whole grains • The new recommendation to significantly reduce refined carbohydrates (roughly 1 in 4 calories in the food supply) is a major change • Incorporate healthy fats from whole foods such as meats, poultry, eggs, seafood, nuts, seeds, full-fat dairy, olives, and avocados • When consuming dairy, include full-fat dairy with no added sugars • Saturated fat consumption should not exceed 10% of calories • An emphasis on healthful fats from whole foods could be beneficial, especially if replacing highly processed foods rich in refined carbohydrates, salt, and other

The recipes are listed alphabetically by primary meal name. All ingredients are given in metric units. Each recipe yields four generous servings unless noted. The mise en place section breaks down pre‑prep tasks into stations, optimising workflow; approximate times are provided. Methods call for just‑in‑time preparation, sensory cues and scientifically informed techniques. “Why this works” offers a brief food‑science explanation. Pairing notes suggest wines or non‑alcoholic beverages that complement the dish and respect the guidelines (moderate alcohol). For optional wine pairings, limit to one glass for women and two for men as advised【32402232832100†L236-L243】.

## Artichoke Benedict with Trout (Peruvian × Nikkei)

**Servings:** 4 **Active time:** 45 min **Total time:** 1 h 15 min

**Mise en place (≈30 min)**
- **Station A – English muffins:** Mix whole‑wheat dough (250 g whole‑wheat flour, 250 g bread flour, 7 g yeast, 10 g sugar, 300 ml warm milk, 30 g butter, 5 g salt) and let proof; shape into 8 muffins, rest 20 min.
- **Station B – Artichokes & trout:** Trim and steam 4 large artichoke hearts (400 g), then slice into quarters; season 200 g smoked trout fillet and flake into bite‑sized pieces.
- **Station C – Hollandaise:** Juice 1 lemon (30 ml), dice 50 g cold butter, measure 3 egg yolks and 50 ml aji‑amarillo purée; set up bain‑marie.
- **Station D – Poaching setup:** Crack 8 fresh eggs into individual ramekins; bring a wide shallow pan of water to a gentle simmer with 30 ml vinegar.
- **Station E – Garnishes:** Chop 30 g chives and 10 g cilantro; prepare aji amarillo hollandaise ingredients and warm plates.

**Ingredients**
- **For the muffins:** As per Station A above.
- **Protein & veg:** 4 steamed artichoke hearts (≈400 g), 200 g smoked trout fillet, 8 large eggs.
- **Hollandaise:** 3 egg yolks, 50 g cold unsalted butter cut into cubes, 30 ml lemon juice, 50 ml aji amarillo purée, 2 ml Dijon mustard, salt to taste.
- **Poaching liquor:** Water, 30 ml white vinegar.
- **Garnish:** Chopped chives, cilantro, freshly ground black pepper.

**Method**
1. **Cook muffins:** Preheat a heavy skillet over medium‑low heat. Roll the rested dough into 2 cm‑thick rounds using a ring cutter. Cook muffins dry (no fat) until golden on each side (≈5 min per side). Split and keep warm.
2. **Steam artichokes:** If not already steamed, cook trimmed hearts in salted boiling water until tender (≈10 min); drain and sear in a hot pan with a drizzle of olive oil until lightly caramelised.
3. **Prepare hollandaise:** In a bain‑marie over barely simmering water, whisk egg yolks with lemon juice and mustard until thick ribbons form. Slowly whisk in cold butter cubes one at a time until emulsified. Add aji amarillo purée; season with salt. Keep warm but not hot to avoid scrambling.
4. **Poach eggs:** Create a gentle vortex in the poaching liquor and slide in one egg at a time. Cook 3 min for runny yolks. Remove with a slotted spoon to a paper towel.
5. **Assemble:** Place a toasted muffin half on each plate. Top with seared artichoke quarters and flaked trout. Gently perch a poached egg on top and spoon over warm aji amarillo hollandaise. Sprinkle with chives, cilantro and black pepper.

**Why this works:** Whole‑wheat muffins provide nutty depth and fibre. Emulsifying butter into egg yolks over gentle heat yields a stable, velvety hollandaise; adding aji amarillo introduces fruity heat and vibrant colour without excess fat. Poaching eggs in acidulated water coagulates the whites quickly for neat spheres, while smoked trout delivers umami and omega‑3s.

**Plating & Pairing:** Serve two halves per person on warm plates. Garnish with micro‑greens for colour. Pair with a glass of sparkling brut nature or a chilled chicha morada spritzer (sparkling water with purple‑corn reduction and lime) for a non‑alcoholic option.

## Birria Ramen with Sous‑Vide Egg (Mexican × Japanese)

**Servings:** 4 **Active time:** 1 h **Total time:** 6 h (includes braising)

**Mise en place (≈40 min)**
- **Station A – Birria broth:** Toast 5 dried guajillo and 3 ancho chiles until fragrant; rehydrate in hot water. Sear 800 g lamb or beef chuck in a Dutch oven; gather aromatics (1 onion, 4 garlic cloves, 2 bay leaves, 5 g cumin seeds, 5 g coriander seeds).
- **Station B – Ramen tare:** Combine 60 ml tamari, 60 ml sake (optional), 30 ml mirin, 30 ml fish sauce and 30 ml rice vinegar.
- **Station C – Noodles & toppings:** Prepare 800 g fresh whole‑wheat ramen noodles; slice 200 g shiitake mushrooms, 100 g radishes, chop 30 g cilantro, slice 2 limes. Set up sous‑vide water bath at 63 °C for eggs.

**Ingredients**
- **Birria:** 800 g grass‑fed lamb or beef chuck cut into chunks, 5 dried guajillo chiles, 3 dried ancho chiles, 1 onion, 4 garlic cloves, 1 stick cinnamon, 2 bay leaves, 5 g each cumin and coriander seeds, 500 ml beef stock, 500 ml water.
- **Ramen:** 800 g fresh whole‑wheat ramen noodles, 4 eggs (for sous‑vide), 200 g shiitake mushrooms, 100 g radishes, 100 g bean sprouts, 30 g cilantro, lime wedges.
- **Tare:** 60 ml tamari, 60 ml sake (omit or use 30 ml extra tamari for non‑alcoholic), 30 ml mirin or apple‑cider vinegar, 30 ml fish sauce, 30 ml rice vinegar.
- **Garnish:** 20 g toasted sesame seeds, 2 spring onions sliced.

**Method**
1. **Make birria:** Toast chiles briefly in a dry pan, then soak in 250 ml boiling water until soft. Blend with soaking liquid, onion, garlic, spices and a pinch of salt to a smooth paste. Sear meat in a Dutch oven until browned; add chile purée, cinnamon stick, bay leaves, stock and water. Bring to a simmer, cover and braise in a 150 °C oven for 4–5 hours until meat is tender. Shred meat and return to broth; adjust salt.
2. **Prepare eggs:** Submerge eggs in a 63 °C sous‑vide bath for 45 min (for jammy yolks). Shock in ice water, then carefully crack and slide into bowls later.
3. **Cook noodles & toppings:** Sauté mushrooms in a drop of sesame oil until browned; season lightly. Blanch ramen noodles in boiling water for 1 min (fresh) or until al dente; rinse briefly to stop cooking.
4. **Assemble bowls:** Place 1 tbsp tare in each warmed bowl. Add noodles. Ladle over hot birria broth and shredded meat. Top with mushrooms, bean sprouts, sliced radish and cilantro. Gently add peeled sous‑vide egg. Finish with sesame seeds, spring onions and a squeeze of lime.

**Why this works:** Slow braising extracts collagen from chuck, producing a silky broth enriched with toasted chiles for deep, complex flavour. The tare concentrates umami (tamari, fish sauce) and balances acidity (vinegar) to season the broth just before serving. Sous‑vide eggs cooked at 63 °C achieve custardy yolks that meld into the soup, echoing the richness of traditional ramen.

**Plating & Pairing:** Serve in deep bowls with long-handled chopsticks and spoons. The broth should be glossy with a gentle chile sheen. Pair with a crisp Kölsch beer (limit to one glass) or a chilled hibiscus‑lime agua fresca.

import re, json
from pathlib import Path

# Read report
report = Path('/home/oai/share/report.md').read_text(encoding='utf-8')

# Extract full recipes section
# We'll extract text between '# 4. Full Recipes' and '# 5.'
start = report.find('# 4. Full Recipes')
end = report.find('# 5. Master Weekly Shopping')
recipes_section = report[start:end]

# Find recipe headings
# Each recipe begins with '## ' followed by name and parenthesis; we will parse accordingly
pattern = r"##\s+(.+?)\n"
# We'll get all names and positions
matches = list(re.finditer(pattern, recipes_section))

recipes = []
for i, match in enumerate(matches):
    name_line = match.group(1).strip()
    # Determine the slice of text belonging to this recipe
    start_idx = match.end()
    end_idx = matches[i+1].start() if i+1 < len(matches) else len(recipes_section)
    content = recipes_section[start_idx:end_idx].strip()
    # Parse sub-sections: We'll attempt to extract Servings/time, Mise en place, Ingredients, Method, Why this works, Plating & Pairing
    # We'll use regex groups to separate sections by '**' or '**Why this works**'
    # Step 1: Servings/time
    servings_match = re.search(r"\*\*Servings:.*?\n", content)
    if not servings_match:
        continue
    servings_line = servings_match.group(0)
    # Extract servings and times using regex
    servings = re.search(r"Servings:\s*(\d+)", servings_line)
    active_time = re.search(r"Active time:\s*([\d\s\w]+)", servings_line)
    total_time = re.search(r"Total time:\s*([\d\s\w]+)", servings_line)
    data = {
        'title': name_line,
        'servings': int(servings.group(1)) if servings else None,
        'active_time': active_time.group(1).strip() if active_time else None,
        'total_time': total_time.group(1).strip() if total_time else None,
    }
    # Mise en place: find between '**Mise' line and '**Ingredients**'
    mise_start = content.find('**Mise')
    ing_start = content.find('**Ingredients')
    if mise_start != -1 and ing_start != -1:
        mise_text = content[mise_start:ing_start]
        # extract bullet lines
        mise_lines = re.findall(r"-\s+([^-]+)", mise_text)
        data['mise_en_place'] = mise_lines
    # Ingredients: from '**Ingredients' to '**Method**'
    method_start = content.find('**Method')
    if ing_start != -1 and method_start != -1:
        ing_text = content[ing_start:method_start]
        # extract bullet lines
        ingredients = re.findall(r"-\s+([^\n]+)", ing_text)
        data['ingredients'] = ingredients
    # Method: from '**Method' to '**Why this works**'
    why_start = content.find('**Why this works')
    if method_start != -1 and why_start != -1:
        method_text = content[method_start:why_start]
        # parse steps lines beginning with digits and period
        steps = re.findall(r"\d+\.\s+([^\n]+)", method_text)
        data['method'] = steps
    # Why this works: from '**Why this works' to '**Plating' or end
    plating_start = content.find('**Plating')
    if why_start != -1:
        end_idx2 = plating_start if plating_start != -1 else len(content)
        why_text = content[why_start:end_idx2]
        data['why_this_works'] = why_text
    # Plating & Pairing: from '**Plating' to end
    if plating_start != -1:
        plating_text = content[plating_start:]
        data['plating'] = plating_text
    recipes.append(data)

print('Extracted', len(recipes), 'recipes')
print(recipes[0].keys())
print(recipes[0]['title'])

PY"]}

## Artichoke Benedict with Trout (Peruvian × Nikkei)

**Servings:** 4 **Active time:** 45 min **Total time:** 1 h 15 min

**Mise en place (≈30 min)**
- **Station A – English muffins:** Mix whole‑wheat dough (250 g whole‑wheat flour, 250 g bread flour, 7 g yeast, 10 g sugar, 300 ml warm milk, 30 g butter, 5 g salt) and let proof; shape into 8 muffins, rest 20 min.
- **Station B – Artichokes & trout:** Trim and steam 4 large artichoke hearts (400 g), then slice into quarters; season 200 g smoked trout fillet and flake into bite‑sized pieces.
- **Station C – Hollandaise:** Juice 1 lemon (30 ml), dice 50 g cold butter, measure 3 egg yolks and 50 ml aji‑amarillo purée; set up bain‑marie.
- **Station D – Poaching setup:** Crack 8 fresh eggs into individual ramekins; bring a wide shallow pan of water to a gentle simmer with 30 ml vinegar.
- **Station E – Garnishes:** Chop 30 g chives and 10 g cilantro; prepare aji amarillo hollandaise ingredients and warm plates.

**Ingredients**
- **For the muffins:** As per Station A above.
- **Protein & veg:** 4 steamed artichoke hearts (≈400 g), 200 g smoked trout fillet, 8 large eggs.
- **Hollandaise:** 3 egg yolks, 50 g cold unsalted butter cut into cubes, 30 ml lemon juice, 50 ml aji amarillo purée, 2 ml Dijon mustard, salt to taste.
- **Poaching liquor:** Water, 30 ml white vinegar.
- **Garnish:** Chopped chives, cilantro, freshly ground black pepper.

**Method**
1. **Cook muffins:** Preheat a heavy skillet over medium‑low heat. Roll the rested dough into 2 cm‑thick rounds using a ring cutter. Cook muffins dry (no fat) until golden on each side (≈5 min per side). Split and keep warm.
2. **Steam artichokes:** If not already steamed, cook trimmed hearts in salted boiling water until tender (≈10 min); drain and sear in a hot pan with a drizzle of olive oil until lightly caramelised.
3. **Prepare hollandaise:** In a bain‑marie over barely simmering water, whisk egg yolks with lemon juice and mustard until thick ribbons form. Slowly whisk in cold butter cubes one at a time until emulsified. Add aji amarillo purée; season with salt. Keep warm but not hot to avoid scrambling.
4. **Poach eggs:** Create a gentle vortex in the poaching liquor and slide in one egg at a time. Cook 3 min for runny yolks. Remove with a slotted spoon to a paper towel.
5. **Assemble:** Place a toasted muffin half on each plate. Top with seared artichoke quarters and flaked trout. Gently perch a poached egg on top and spoon over warm aji amarillo hollandaise. Sprinkle with chives, cilantro and black pepper.

**Why this works:** Whole‑wheat muffins provide nutty depth and fibre. Emulsifying butter into egg yolks over gentle heat yields a stable, velvety hollandaise; adding aji amarillo introduces fruity heat and vibrant colour without excess fat. Poaching eggs in acidulated water coagulates the whites quickly for neat spheres, while smoked trout delivers umami and omega‑3s.

**Plating & Pairing:** Serve two halves per person on warm plates. Garnish with micro‑greens for colour. Pair with a glass of sparkling brut nature or a chilled chicha morada spritzer (sparkling water with purple‑corn reduction and lime) for a non‑alcoholic option.
